title: Vertical Order Traversal of a Binary Tree
description: Brute force to optimized: BFS grouping without a tie-break sort versus DFS coordinate collection sorted by column, row, and value.

sections.title: Vertical Order Traversal of a Binary Tree

content.title: Vertical Order Traversal of a Binary Tree

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the root of a binary tree, compute its vertical order traversal: nodes are grouped by column (assigning the root column 0, left child column minus one, right child column plus one), ordered left to right by column; within the same column, ordered top to bottom by row, and for nodes at the SAME row and column, ordered by their value ascending.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","root of a binary tree"],["Output","A list of lists, one per column left to right, each ordered by row then value"],["Key Insight","Every node has a well-defined (row, column) coordinate; going left decreases the column, going right increases it, and going down always increases the row"],["Constraints","Up to 1000 nodes"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Group nodes by vertical column\"","Assigning a (row, column) coordinate to every node via DFS or BFS, then sorting by (column, row, value) to get the exact required order"],["\"Ties at the same row and column broken by value\"","A stable, explicit multi-key sort (column first, then row, then value) is needed, since simple BFS grouping alone does not guarantee this tie-breaking order"]]}

blocks.text: Every node can be assigned a coordinate: the root starts at (row 0, column 0); moving to a left child increases the row by 1 and decreases the column by 1; moving to a right child increases the row by 1 and increases the column by 1. Collecting every node's (column, row, value), then sorting first by column, then by row, then by value (to break ties at the same row and column), produces exactly the grouping and ordering required.

blocks.title: Analogy: Organizing Photos on a Wall by Vertical Strip, Then Height, Then Timestamp
blocks.text: Picture photos pinned to a wall, each with a horizontal strip position and a vertical height. Organizing them strip by strip (left to right), and within a strip from top to bottom, and for photos at the exact same spot breaking ties by their timestamp, produces a precise, unambiguous arrangement.

blocks.caption: Assign every node a (row, column) coordinate: left child row+1 col-1, right child row+1 col+1

blocks.text: Result: [[4],[2],[1,5,6],[3],[7]]. Nodes 5 and 6 share row 2, column 0, so they are ordered by value ascending: 5 before 6.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Every node has a well-defined column and row, computable via a simple DFS or BFS that tracks (row, column) as it descends, starting from (0, 0) at the root.

Observation 2: Collecting every node's (column, row, value) triple during this traversal captures everything needed to answer the query.

Observation 3: Sorting ALL collected triples by column first (to group nodes into their vertical strips, left to right), then by row (top to bottom within a strip), then by value (to deterministically break ties at the exact same row and column), produces precisely the required output order.

Observation 4: Grouping the sorted triples by their column value (consecutive triples sharing the same column) then extracts the final list of lists directly.
This leads to a DFS (or BFS) collecting every node's (column, row, value), followed by an explicit sort on (column, row, value), then grouping by column.
Use BFS, grouping nodes by column as levels are processed, but WITHOUT a final explicit sort to correctly break ties between nodes sharing the exact same row and column.

codes.python:
def vertical_traversal_incomplete(root):
    from collections import defaultdict, deque
    col_map = defaultdict(list)
    queue = deque([(root, 0)])
    while queue:
        node, col = queue.popleft()
        if node is None:
            continue
        col_map[col].append(node.val)                      # appended in BFS order, NOT value-sorted for ties
        queue.append((node.left, col - 1))
        queue.append((node.right, col + 1))
    return [col_map[c] for c in sorted(col_map)]

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Grouping by column during BFS directly captures the column dimension simply.
This does not correctly order nodes that share the exact same row AND column by their value, a requirement this approach misses without an explicit final sort.

blocks.text: Limitation: collecting (column, row, value) triples explicitly and sorting by all three keys correctly handles the value-based tie-breaking requirement that plain BFS grouping misses.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Run a DFS (or BFS) from the root at (row 0, column 0), recording every node's (column, row, value) triple into a shared list; moving to a left child uses (row+1, column-1), moving to a right child uses (row+1, column+1). After the traversal, sort the ENTIRE list of triples by column ascending, then row ascending, then value ascending (this correctly breaks ties for nodes sharing the same row and column). Finally, group consecutive triples sharing the same column into the final list of lists.
Collect every node's (column, row, value), sort by all three keys, then group by column.
Dry run for [1,2,3,4,5,6,7] (1 with children 2,3; 2 with 4,5; 3 with 6,7)
5 and 6 share (column 0, row 2), so sorting by value breaks the tie: 5 comes before 6.

codes.python:
def vertical_traversal(root):
    items = []
    def dfs(node, row, col):
        if node is None:
            return
        items.append((col, row, node.val))
        dfs(node.left, row + 1, col - 1)
        dfs(node.right, row + 1, col + 1)
    dfs(root, 0, 0)
    items.sort()                                              # sorts by (col, row, val) automatically via tuple ordering
    result = []
    cur_col = None
    for col, row, val in items:
        if col != cur_col:
            result.append([])
            cur_col = col
        result[-1].append(val)
    return result

blocks.text: Assigning every node its exact (column, row) coordinate via DFS correctly captures its horizontal grouping and vertical order relative to every other node; sorting the complete list of (column, row, value) triples using ALL THREE keys, in that priority order, guarantees columns are grouped left to right, rows within a column are ordered top to bottom, and any remaining ties (same row and column) are deterministically broken by value ascending, exactly matching the problem's required ordering.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n) for the sort, dominating the O(n) DFS.
Space: O(n) for the collected triples.

blocks.text: Vertical Order Traversal of a Binary Tree tests careful handling of a subtle tie-breaking rule: an explicit multi-key sort is required to correctly order nodes sharing the exact same position.

items: Grouping by column via BFS alone without a final explicit sort, which fails to correctly order nodes sharing the exact same row and column by value.
Forgetting that "row" must strictly increase going DOWN the tree, not being confused with the column dimension.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["Multiple nodes sharing the exact same row and column","Ordered by their value ascending, as the final tie-breaker."],["A single node tree","A single column containing just that one value."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "sort by column, then row, then value, in that exact priority order" heads off the most common subtle bug in this problem before writing any code.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "group tree nodes by vertical column, breaking ties carefully", think: assign (row, column) coordinates via DFS, then sort by (column, row, value).

items: How would this differ from "Binary Tree Vertical Order Traversal" (an easier variant that breaks ties by BFS order instead of value)?
Binary Tree Level Order Traversal, which shares the underlying idea of assigning coordinates during a traversal.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The BFS-only grouping approach costs O(n) but is INCORRECT for the value-based tie-break requirement; the DFS-plus-multi-key-sort approach costs O(n log n), the standard fully correct solution.

items: Pattern: assign (row, column) coordinates via DFS, then sort by an explicit multi-key priority (column, row, value).
Core Idea: left decreases column, right increases column, down always increases row; ties at the same coordinate break by value.
Time: O(n) for the incomplete BFS grouping, O(n log n) for the fully correct sorted approach.
Most Important Observation: an explicit multi-key sort is required, since BFS order alone does not guarantee the value-based tie-break.
Interview Difficulty: a hard problem due to its subtle tie-breaking requirement.
One line memory trick: sort by column, then row, then value.
